# Perpetual-to-Subscription Transition Plan
## Moving the Business Model Without Losing the Installed Base, the Sales Force, or the Board

*Executable plan with working tools: offer architecture, migration math, comp mechanics, guidance skeletons, one-glance timeline. Bracketed figures are placeholders to be set from your model — the relationships between them are the plan. The competitor's 20% installed-base loss was not bad luck; it was a design choice. This plan is built from its autopsy.*

---

## 1. Strategic Frame

**Situation:** Perpetual licenses plus paid upgrades produce lumpy, heavily discounted revenue. Leadership wants subscriptions. The obstacles are a multi-year revenue trough, a sales force paid on upfront deals, and an installed base that believes — correctly — that it owns what it bought.

**Strategic reality:** The trough is not avoidable; it is the price of admission, and it is *chosen, not suffered*. Depth and duration trade against each other, and both are set by decisions you control. What is not survivable is a trough the board didn't pre-approve, investors didn't pre-model, or customers experience as confiscation. Adobe's revenue fell and its stock rose through its trough because every decline was pre-announced and every quarter beat a published subscription metric. The competitor lost a fifth of its base because it forced migration. Those two facts are the whole strategy.

**Transition arc:** 2 quarters to prepare the scoreboard → 4–6 quarters of descent → trough bottom around quarter [6–8] → ARR crosses the old revenue baseline around quarter [10–12] → full recovery and re-rating by year 3.

**Operating principles:**

1. **Never force the installed base.** Customers forgive a price; they do not forgive a confiscation. Every perpetual license keeps working, contractually, in writing, forever. Migration must be voluntary and economically obvious.
2. **Sell the future, not the switch.** Subscription must be a better product — continuous delivery, cloud services, collaboration — not the same bits with a different invoice. A model change without product change is a price increase, and customers will say so.
3. **Change the scoreboard before the numbers move.** Investors panic when you report declines in the metrics they value. Give them ARR, mix, and retention two quarters *before* the trough, and the declines arrive pre-forgiven.
4. **Reps sell their comp plan, not your strategy.** Compensation is redesigned and announced before launch, not patched after the first bad quarter.
5. **Promise the downside, plan to the base.** The published model is a covenant. Print the pessimistic case; beat it.
6. **Announce the destination, not just the departure.** A firm end state for perpetual (feature freeze, end-of-sale for new logos) prevents indefinite straddling — but the end state is about *new* sales, never about existing licenses.

---

## 2. Design the Trough — Depth vs. Duration Is One Dial

Pricing aggressiveness and perpetual's end-of-sale date are the same control: faster conversion kills license revenue sooner (deeper trough, faster ARR build); slower conversion stretches the decline. Model three scenarios and choose explicitly:

| Scenario | Perpetual end-of-sale (new logos) | Migration incentives | Peak revenue decline | Trough duration | Churn risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A — Aggressive** | Immediate | Rich, short window | [20–30]% | ~5–6 quarters | **Highest — this is the competitor's path** |
| **B — Base (recommended)** | Month [12] | Strong, stepping down over [24–36] months | [12–18]% | ~7–8 quarters | Managed |
| **C — Slow** | Month [24+] | Modest | [6–10]% | 10–12+ quarters | Lowest churn, highest **drift risk** |

**Why not A:** it is the documented failure — forced migration, price shock, no grandfathering, 20% of the base walks.
**Why not C:** two parallel sales motions for years is comp-plan hell; investors and employees lose faith in a transition with no visible destination; competitors out-flank while you straddle.

**The most dangerous moment is quarter [6–8]:** license revenue is gone, ARR is not yet visibly compounding, skeptics are loudest. This is when boards lose nerve, CEOs get fired, and strategies get reversed at the exact bottom. The antidote is pre-commitment: the trough bottom is named in the published model, and the response to it is written in advance (Section 7).

**Cash note — the most reassuring true sentence in the deck:** with annual upfront billing, billings exceed recognized revenue during the ramp and deferred revenue builds. The cash trough is materially shallower than the P&L trough. Say this explicitly and early; then size liquidity to the P&L trough *plus* accelerated comp payouts (Section 5) plus two quarters of slack.

---

## 3. Offer Structure & Migration Incentives

### Three lanes, no dead ends

| Lane | Who | Terms |
|---|---|---|
| **Subscription (flagship)** | Everyone; default for new logos from launch, exclusive for new logos from month [12] | Continuous updates, cloud services, support; annual or multi-year, billed upfront |
| **Perpetual (frozen)** | Existing holders; new buyers until month [12] | Version [N] is the final feature release; security/critical fixes through [date]; maintenance repriced upward annually |
| **Regulated / offline (permanent)** | Air-gapped, embedded, compliance-bound customers who *cannot* subscribe | Perpetual + extended support lane, premium-priced, explicitly permanent |

The third lane is the difference between 2% attrition and 20%. Some customers cannot move to a cloud-tethered model, and forcing them converts them into the competitor's reference accounts. Give them a dignified, expensive, permanent home.

### Segment the installed base — it is not monolithic

| Segment | Share | Treatment |
|---|---|---|
| Current on maintenance | [40–55]% | Best migration terms; named-account migration quotas |
| Lapsed maintenance, recent version | [—]% | Reinstatement amnesty, then standard bridge offer |
| Old versions, static usage | [—]% | Leave alone. Hospice support. No chase |
| Regulated / offline | [—]% | Permanent lane above |
| New logos | — | Subscription-only from month [12] |

### The migration offer

- **The pledge, first and always:** "Your license is yours. It will keep working." Contractual, written, before any incentive is discussed.
- **The bridge:** customers current on maintenance move at [their current maintenance rate + ~25%] for years 1–2, stepping to list by year [3–4]. Lapsed customers get a one-time amnesty window.
- **The incentive curve slopes down:** richest terms in months 1–12, stepping down at months [12] and [24]. The deadline applies to the *discount*, never to the *right to stay*.
- **Multi-year locks:** 3-year price locks for prepaid multi-year conversions — reduces renewal risk, builds RPO, and gives investors visible contracted revenue.
- **Discount discipline:** never discount subscription *list* price. Use expiring migration credits. Discounts expire; list prices don't — and renewal economics anchor to list.
